Before Badr the Prophet consults his companions and Sa'd b. Ubada pledges to follow him anywhere; a captured water-carrier is beaten, and the Prophet marks where each enemy will fall.
Taking Mecca, the Prophet assures the Ansar he will live and die with them, strikes the idols round the Ka'bah, and says no Quraishite will henceforth be killed bound.
Ali writes the Hudaybiyya treaty and the Prophet himself strikes out 'Messenger of Allah', accepting the Meccans' terms; Umar objects, and a surah of victory is revealed.
Hudhaifa and his father, caught by Quraish on the way to Badr, promised not to fight with the Prophet, who told them to keep that promise and seek Allah's help.
On a bitterly cold, windy night of Ahzab the Prophet sends Hudhaifa to bring news of the enemy without provoking them; he holds back from shooting Abu Sufyan and returns.
At Uhud Ansar die defending the wounded Prophet, whose bleeding Fatima stops; he asks how his attackers can be saved, and recalls a prophet who asked forgiveness for his people.
Quraish lay a camel's foetus on the prostrating Prophet and he invokes Allah against their chiefs, later slain at Badr; rejected at Aqaba, he spares his people; his finger bleeds.
When Gabriel delayed and the Prophet, ill, did not rise for night prayer, polytheists said he was forsaken, and Allah revealed that his Lord had not forsaken him.
Abdullah b. Ubayy rebuffs the Prophet's call and the two sides quarrel; the Prophet calms them and forgives him, and a verse on making peace between quarrelling believers comes.
After Badr Ibn Mas'ud finds Abu Jahl dying, struck down by the two sons of Afra, and Abu Jahl laments that farmers killed him.
The Prophet asks who will kill Ka'b b. Ashraf for maligning Allah and His Messenger; Muhammad b. Maslama draws him out with a loan ruse and his party kills him.
The Prophet raids Khaibar at dawn, foretelling its ruin, and takes it; Amir b. al-Akwa', the march's poet, dies by his own sword yet has a double reward.
Carrying earth while digging the ditch, the Prophet chants verses with his companions, praying that, since true life is the Hereafter's, Allah forgive and help the Ansar and Muhajirs.
Salama b. al-Akwa' pledges allegiance thrice at Hudaybiyya, recovers the Prophet's camels from raiders at Dhu Qarad alone and sees Ali take Khaibar; attacking Meccans are captured and spared.
Umm Sulaim bears a dagger at Hunain; Ansar women go to war to give water and treat the wounded; at Uhud Abu Talha shields the Prophet while women carry water.
Ibn Abbas answers Najda: women and slaves get booty gifts, not shares; enemy children are not killed; orphanhood ends at maturity; the fifth for the Prophet's kin was denied them.
Umm Atiyya took part in seven battles with the Prophet, staying in the camp to cook, treat the wounded and nurse the sick.
Companions count the Prophet's expeditions, nineteen by several reports with fighting in eight, and Abu Musa tells how the Dhat ar-Riqa' expedition was named for their rag-bound feet.
On the way to Badr the Prophet twice turns away a brave polytheist seeking to join for booty, taking no help from a polytheist, and accepts him once he believes.
People follow the Quraish in good and evil, the Caliphate stays with them, and Islam remains strong until twelve caliphs, all from Quraish, have ruled.
Wounded, Umar indicates he will name no successor, as the Prophet named none though Abu Bakr did, despite his son's warning that the people would be left untended.
The Prophet says not to ask for authority and appoints none who seek it; Abu Dharr is weak, and office is a trust bringing regret on Judgement Day unless fulfilled.
The just will sit on pulpits of light near Allah, and the Prophet prayed that Allah be hard on rulers hard on his people and kind to the kind.
Everyone is a shepherd answerable for his flock; a ruler who dies cheating or neglecting his people is barred from Paradise, and the cruel ruler is the worst.
Whoever misappropriates booty or public funds, even a needle, will carry it on Judgement Day; an official who claimed as his own gifts given him while collecting charity is rebuked.
The verse on obeying those in authority came about a commander the Prophet sent; whoever obeys the Prophet obeys Allah, and whoever obeys his commander obeys him.
Muslims must listen to and obey the ruler in hardship and ease, even when others are preferred, and even a maimed Abyssinian slave who leads by Allah's Book.
Obedience to a ruler holds except in sin: those who refused a commander's order to enter a fire were right; companions pledged to obey in all conditions save clear disbelief.
The ruler is a shield; many caliphs will follow the Prophet, the first given allegiance taking precedence; amid coming trials one obeys them, but not in disobeying Allah.
An Ansari who asked for office was told to bear favouritism after the Prophet patiently until the Cistern; rulers who withhold people's rights must be obeyed, each bearing his burden.
Hudhaifa asked about evil times ahead; the Prophet foretold callers at Hell's gates and leaders not following his guidance, and said to keep with the Muslims' main body and Amir.
Whoever leaves obedience and the main body, dies with no oath of allegiance, or is killed under a blind banner for his tribe dies the death of Jahiliyya.
Whoever seeks to split the community united under one leader is to be killed, and when allegiance is given to two caliphs, the later one is to be killed.
Rulers will do good and bad: whoever hates their wrongs is blameless, whoever approves them is ruined, and while they establish prayer, none may fight them or withdraw obedience.
At Hudaibiya thirteen to fifteen hundred pledged allegiance under the tree, not to die fighting but never to flee; the Prophet called them the best people on earth.
Next year those who pledged could not find the tree; Salama said they pledged to die fighting, and Abdullah b. Zaid would make no such pledge after the Prophet.
No emigration remains after the conquest of Mecca, only jihad and intention; the Prophet let Salama live in the desert and told a Bedouin paying zakat to keep doing good.
The Prophet took the pledge of the believing women who emigrated by spoken word on the terms of the Quranic verse, and his hand never touched a woman's hand.
Companions pledged to the Prophet to hear and obey, and he had them add: as far as it lies in my power.
Ibn Umar was turned away from fighting at Uhud aged fourteen and allowed at the Trench aged fifteen, which Umar b. Abd al-Aziz made the line between minor and adult.
